inputs.original_text:
Tens of thousands marched through central London on Saturday, bringing trade unions, anti-racism campaigners and Muslim representative bodies together against the far right. That solidarity is a powerful refusal to let targeted communities be isolated or blamed for problems rooted in inequality and insecurity.

But marches and condemnations are not enough. Far-right politics thrives when people are left without security and when institutions fail to challenge the conditions that make scapegoating appealing. With key local elections only weeks away, protecting targeted communities must go hand in hand with reforms that tackle those deeper injustices.
inputs.modified_text:
Tens of thousands marched through central London on Saturday, with trade unions, anti-racism campaigners and Muslim representative bodies standing together against the far right. That unity matters: targeted communities should not be left to face scapegoating alone.

But solidarity has to mean more than a march. Far-right politics feeds on insecurity and on institutions that fail to confront the inequalities behind it. As key local elections approach in weeks, protecting people from discrimination must go alongside serious reforms that make life more secure and challenge those deeper injustices.
